prerequisites: Basic knowledge of Chemistry (from first-year Chemistry and second-year Advanced Chemistry)
Basic knowledge of Thermodynamics (from first-year Mechanics and Thermodynamics, second-year Thermal Engineering, and third-year Applied Chemical Thermodynamics for Engineering)
Basic knowledge of Chemical Kinetics (from third-year Chemical Kinetics and Reactors)
Basic knowledge of Materials Science (from second-year Materials Science)

learning_outcomes.text: Understand the basic unifying principles of all Electrochemistry (principles of ionics and electrodics; equilibrium and dynamic) and distinguish them from experimental techniques and the specific details of each application.
Apply basic principles to estimate and measure the service life of metals in aggressive environments and to obtain a unified understanding of methods to combat electrochemical corrosion.

Apply basic principles to the problem of clean energy generation using batteries and fuel cells, verifying that the efficiencies of electrochemical energy generation exceed those of conventional thermal machines.
Apply basic principles to unify various industrial electrochemical processes, with emphasis on those present in the industrial activity of the environment.

syllabus_topics: General introduction to non-equilibrium: overpotential and electrode processes.
Coupled equations for ionic transport in dilute solutions.
Current-voltage relationships for a galvanic cell.

Introduction: economic aspects and types of metallic corrosion by morphology (generalized, localized, galvanic, pitting, intergranular, SCC, fatigue corrosion, embrittlement, etc.) and mechanism (electrochemical and high temperature).
Corrosion cell model: corrosion potential and current.
Identification of anodic and cathodic zones in a metal.
Thermodynamics of corrosion (differential aeration, Nernst analytical criterion, Pourbaix diagrams, limitations).
Kinetics of corrosion: electrochemical measurement of corrosion rate by fitting to mixed potential theory (Wagner and Stern-Geary).
Kinetics of corrosion: interpretations using Evans diagrams.
Prevention, inhibition, and control of corrosion.
Lesson 4.- Electrochemical Batteries and Industrial Applications of Electrochemistry.
Introduction: commercialized batteries and fuel cells.
Calculation of maximum or ideal characteristics (capacities, energies, and densities) in commercial systems.
Measurement of real characteristics (Q, W, P) through discharge curves.
Charge curves at constant I (overcharge and recombination, efficiencies).
Charge and discharge cycles: memory and alloy effects in NiCad and aging mechanisms in Li-ion.
Efficiencies of galvanic and fuel cells in energy conversion.
Theoretical description of some industrial electrochemical processes (electrodeposition, surface finishes, electrosynthesis, etc.), with emphasis on performance parameters.

assessment_methods.method: Written exams with questions and problems
Defense of classroom practice exercises and short tests

assessment_rules: For the ordinary call, if all minimums of 4.0 in P1, P2 or F are met, the final grade is calculated either by partials (0.35x(P1+P2) + 0.1xPA + 0.05xENT + 0.15xTG) or by final exam (0.7xF + 0.1xPA + 0.05xENT + 0.15xTG). A minimum final grade of 5.0 is required to pass; otherwise, the grade is the minimum of the calculated score and 4.0. For extraordinary calls and differentiated evaluation (part-time students), the assessment is a 100% written final exam covering all material; continuous assessment components and approved partials are not considered.
